title: E2E tracebook: latency histogram deep-dive
content:
Summary:

This is a working tracebook capturing an end-to-end latency profiling run against the staging A100 fleet (us-west2) for rw-13b-int8 variants. The goal was to map p50/p95/p99 behavior to per-stage timing and surface the principal tail contributors so we can prioritize short-term mitigations. This is intentionally informal — reproductions, trace ids and hypotheses are below.

Quick headline numbers (sample: 10k traces over 24h, sampled at ~10% of requests):
- Overall E2E (client->response): p50 = 48 ms, p95 = 320 ms, p99 = 1.02 s
- Observed multi-modal distribution: large cluster around 40–70 ms, secondary cluster (queuing) around 300–400 ms, tail events up to 2.5 s.

Environment/experiment details:
- Region: us-west2 (staging), node type: A100-SXM4 80GB, CUDA 12.2 driver
- Model: rwkv-13b-int8 (dynamic quant), KV-cache enabled for prompt prefixing
- Request profile: mix of short chat turns (seq_len 64) and long completion requests (seq_len up to 1500); ~78% short, 22% long
- Ingress: nginx LB -> envoy router -> serving-runtime worker (single-GPU process)
- Batching config: dynamic batching enabled, max_batch_size=32, max_batch_latency_ms=12
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry spans, Jaeger collector, sampled traces enriched with kernel-level BPF hist for host<->GPU memcpy (recent kernel probe)
- Dataset: 10k traces chosen to evenly cover traffic hours (spike between 10:00–14:00 PST)

Per-stage aggregated (p50 / p95 / p99) — numbers in ms and short notes on behavior:
- Ingress (nginx accept + TLS handshake): 3 / 9 / 20 — small contribution, stable
- Network hop (LB -> worker): 2 / 6 / 14 — negligible variability
- Envoy routing: 4 / 12 / 38 — occasional routing delays due to hot path CPU contention on router pod (see notes)
- Scheduler wait (worker queuing before kernel): 6 / 84 / 360 — major tail contributor; queuing spikes correlate with bursts of long-seq requests and when max_batch_size reaches 32
- Kernel compute (GPU compute + kernel launches): 22 / 170 / 470 — second major tail; p99 events show stalls and repeated kernel retries (suspect memory/launch contention on long sequences)
- KV-cache lookup & prefixing: 1 / 4 / 12 — small, except when prefix size > 4096 tokens (rare)
- Host->Device memcpy: 2 / 8 / 30 — in p99 this moves to 100+ ms when pinned-memory pool is saturated (see BPF traces)
- Token encode/pack/response serialize: 4 / 16 / 28
- Streaming flush to client: 4 / 6 / 12

Interpretation / what the numbers mean:
- Scheduler queueing (p95->p99 gap) accounts for ~35–45% of the heavy-tail events. The queue increases when long-seq requests enter the pipeline and hit dynamic batching thresholds; batches inflate and one long-seq inflates average per-token work, stalling short requests behind it.
- Kernel compute p99 shows both longer compute and gaps due to kernel launch backoff. BPF traces show occasional repeated small GPU kernel launches that are spaced out (gaps of 20–80 ms), consistent with context switches or preemption at the driver level.
- Host->Device memcpy spikes coincide with host memory pressure on the worker: pinned memory pool exhaustion leads to fallback to pageable copies which are much slower. This lines up with times where several concurrent long-seq requests are being prepared for a single batch.

Example trace snippets (representative ids):
- trace-1a7f3: overall 57 ms — clean path, batch size 4, seq=64, kernel=25 ms, queue=5 ms
- trace-4c9b2: overall 395 ms — queue=240 ms (waiting for batch), kernel compute=130 ms, memcpy=11 ms
- trace-b2d09: overall 1.9 s — queue=520 ms, kernel stalls with repeated 80–120 ms gaps (observed 3 times), memcpy fallback = 420 ms

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Dynamic batching interaction with heterogeneous seq lengths (long-seq requests pull up batch processing time) => increases queueing for short requests, causing secondary tail.
2) Pinned-memory pool is too small relative to concurrent long-seq work => some memcopies fall back to pageable and blow up memcpy times.
3) Kernel preemption/context-switches on GPU when concurrent kernels + CUDA driver versions cause launch serialization. Might be triggered by debug metrics or CUDA stream scheduling.
4) Router/Envoy CPU hot spots add variability but are not the main tail cause.

Quick experiments & results (short-run):
- Experiment A: cap_max_batch_size=12 (staging) for 2h window (same midday traffic): p95 dropped from 320 ms -> 210 ms, p99 from 1.02 s -> 640 ms. Queue p95 reduced by ~50%. However throughput (tokens/sec) decreased by ~12% and avg GPU utilization dropped 6%.
- Experiment B: increase pinned-memory pool by 2x on worker hosts and restart workers: observed host->device memcpy p99 fall from 420 ms -> 38 ms on affected traces; overall p99 improved ~180 ms. Side effects: slightly higher host memory usage; no OOM observed in 6h test.
- Experiment C: applied sequence-length-based routing (route seq>1024 to dedicated long-seq queue with max_batch_size=4): tail events for short requests nearly vanished in the test window; long-seq p99 remained high but isolated. This requires routing logic changes in router and small deploy.

Short-term recommended mitigations (low risk):
- Reduce max_batch_size to 12 for mixed workloads by default, and auto-scale up for sustained short-only traffic. Owner: Benji (eng-serving-runtime).
- Increase pinned-memory pool size on staging and run for 48h; monitor memcpy p99. Owner: Miguel (infra).
- Implement a seq_len header and routing rule to route >1024 requests to a separate worker pool or dedicate small-batch workers. Owner: Zoe (platform).

Medium-term (investigate):
- Work with driver team to reproduce kernel launch gaps; capture per-GPU occupancy and driver logs for p99 traces and open ticket with NVIDIA if needed. Owner: Aisha + SRE.
- Evaluate adaptive batching that considers estimated per-request compute (e.g., expected tokens to generate) rather than raw count. Prototype in a canary route. Owner: eng-serving-runtime research.

Open questions / things to validate:
- Are any customer-side gRPC keepalive settings causing request bundling (we saw a small correlation to clients that use old SDK versions)?
- Do any logs show OOM or throttling in the CUDA driver during the large kernel-stall traces? We have partial logs; need full driver debug logs for 3 representative p99 traces.
- Is the pinned memory exhaustion pattern appearing in production (hosted) or limited to staging due to co-located test jobs?

Next steps / action items (short list):
- [ ] Benji: roll max_batch_size=12 config to canary fleet by 2025-02-14 and collect 24h traces.
- [ ] Miguel: increase pinned-memory pool on staging hosts; provide memory pressure metrics dashboard by 2025-02-15.
- [ ] Zoe: prototype seq-length header routing; spec doc due 2025-02-20.
- [ ] Aisha: collect full driver logs for 3 p99 trace ids and coordinate with SRE to reproduce gaps.

Notes / misc:
- This doc intentionally mixes notes + early test results; treat as working. If anything here becomes product/tenant-impacting we should escalate to SRE oncall and the incident channel.
- Saved search filter used for traces: service:serving-runtime AND env:staging AND duration_ms >= 250

Appendix: raw histogram buckets (summary, counts from sample 10k) — bucket edges (ms) and counts:
- 0-50 ms: 6,820 (68.2%)
- 50-200 ms: 2,150 (21.5%)
- 200-500 ms: 780 (7.8%)
- 500-1000 ms: 170 (1.7%)
- 1000+ ms: 80 (0.8%)

If you want raw trace exports or the jaeger sample set I used, ping me and I'll dump a json bundle (about 42 MB) to the shared staging bucket.

-- Aisha
